  "text": "The laundrette on Bell Street had seven machines, but only six appeared in the window’s reflection.

I noticed while waiting for my sheets.

Number four was missing.

An old man folding towels caught me looking.

“Never use that one for anything you want back,” he said.

My sheets were in number four.

Through its round door, something pale pressed against the glass. A fitted corner, I thought. Then it spread five fingers.

I hit the stop button.

The drum kept turning.

The old man gathered his towels, leaving one behind.

“Wait until it finishes,” he said. “Don’t make it open early.”

He left before I could ask what he meant.

The display read ONE MINUTE.

For twenty minutes, it read ONE MINUTE.

Then my phone buzzed.

A photograph from my sister: her spare bedroom, freshly painted. She wanted my opinion.

In the background, our mother was making the bed.

We had buried her wearing the blue cardigan she had on in the photograph.

“Where did you get this?” I typed.

The machine chimed.

Its door swung open.

Inside lay my sheets, dry and neatly folded. They smelled of my childhood home: lavender soap, cigarette smoke, the damp cupboard beneath the stairs.

My sister replied.

“What photograph?”

Behind me, someone shook out the towel the old man had left.

“You always leave everything till the last minute,” my mother said.

I watched the shop window.

Six machines. One person.

Her hands settled on my shoulders, warm and heavy.

“Come on,” she said. “Help me fold this.”

In the glass, the towel lifted and stretched itself between two empty spaces."
